Project 1

New Zealand Electricity Demand — Statistical Inference, Machine Learning & Forecasting

R · Python · Power BI · Machine Learning

PGDAV8.100 Data Analytics & Visualisation, Master of IT, Eastern Institute of Technology — Oct to Dec 2026 (in progress)

Scenario-based academic project using publicly available data: the analysis takes the role of a data analyst supporting New Zealand’s system operator, generators and retailers. All cleaning, analysis, tables and figures are produced from untouched raw files by a reproducible R script.

Electricity supply must match demand every half-hour, so under-forecasting risks shortages and over-forecasting wastes generation capacity. I combined five years of national demand, wholesale price, temperature and holiday data to measure what drives daily demand, then built and tested forecasting models against a naive benchmark and added prediction intervals so planners see a range, not just a single number.

Data Integration Feature Engineering Hypothesis Testing Regression Time-Series Forecasting Model Validation Conformal Prediction Power BI Dashboard DAX Measures
87,648Half-hourly records (Oct 2021–Sep 2026)
77%Workday demand variation explained by temperature
1.40%Day-ahead forecast error (MAPE)
63%Error reduction vs naive benchmark
  • Integrated half-hourly demand and wholesale price data (Electricity Authority EMI), daily temperatures for Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin (Open-Meteo) and a public holiday calendar into a 1,826-day analytical table, with zero duplicate periods and 0.5% incomplete days excluded with justification.
  • Engineered features including heating degree days (13 °C base), calendar flags (weekend, public holiday, Christmas–New Year, season), an annual seasonal curve and lagged demand.
  • Tested demand drivers statistically: workday demand averaged 117.5 GWh against 107.0 GWh on weekends, a 10.5 GWh (about 9%) difference with a large effect size (Mann–Whitney U, Welch t-test, Cohen’s d = 1.34). Each extra heating degree day added 3.82 GWh, reported with Newey–West intervals after diagnosing autocorrelated residuals.
  • Built and compared 11 forecasting models — linear regression, lasso, SARIMA, gradient boosting and random forest — trained on 2022–2025 and tested on a hold-out year, with expanding-window cross-validation and Diebold–Mariano tests. A well-specified linear model (1.40% MAPE) matched or beat the machine learning models, which overfitted on four years of daily data.
  • Quantified uncertainty with 80% split-conformal prediction intervals (±2.5 GWh, 77% coverage) and identified a key risk: coverage fell to 58% on cold-snap days, so winter reserve needs extra margin until intervals are calibrated separately for cold days.
  • Communicated results through a four-page Power BI dashboard (Forecast, Accuracy, Horizon, Drivers) and written reports translating findings into planning decisions.

Power BI Dashboard

A four-page interactive dashboard with season, day-type and date slicers, page navigation and DAX measures (MAPE, benchmark error, error reduction and interval coverage).

Project 2

Smart Home Automation App for Older Adults — Usability Evaluation

Figma · Maze · Usability Testing

ITPG8.600 Advanced Mobile & Wireless Technologies, Master of IT, Eastern Institute of Technology — 2026

Team project (Sprints 1–5: research, personas, wireframes and prototype design). This case study focuses on my individually authored Sprint 6 deliverable: the usability test plan, evaluation and critical report.

Evaluated a mobile app prototype designed to help independent senior adults (aged 66–86) manage lighting, temperature, security and emergency alerts at home, for a retirement village context. I planned and ran a remote usability test using Maze, analysed the results against the design decisions from earlier sprints, and produced a critical comparison against voice-only assistants and AI-based smart home systems.

100%Task success rate (3 core tasks)
0%Drop-off & misclick rate

5Participants, aged 66–86
  • Designed and ran a remote Maze usability test across 3 core task flows (switch on light, increase room temperature, send SOS alert) with 5 participants representing varied technical proficiency and mobility levels.
  • Analysed quantitative metrics (success rate, drop-off, misclicks, task duration, Maze score) alongside qualitative participant feedback, finding a 100% task completion rate with no errors.
  • Critically reviewed the prototype's design choices, information architecture and accessibility features against personas and requirements defined in earlier sprints.
  • Benchmarked the solution against voice-only assistants (Alexa, Google Assistant) and AI-based automation systems, concluding a hybrid approach best serves senior users' need for visibility, trust and caregiver support.

Project 3

NYC Airbnb Market Data Analysis

Python · Pandas · NumPy · Matplotlib

Academic Project — Graduate Certificate in Cyber Security, University of Adelaide, 2025

Analysed a public dataset of 48,895 Airbnb listings across New York City to uncover pricing patterns and their relationship with guest engagement (number of reviews), using Python's data science stack end-to-end — from raw CSV to cleaned dataset to visual insight.

Data Cleaning Descriptive Statistics Groupby Aggregation Data Visualisation
  • Cleaned a 48,895-row, 16-column dataset by identifying and removing rows/columns with missing values (e.g. last_review, reviews_per_month).
  • Computed summary statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, quartiles) for rental price (mean $152.72, median $106) and number of reviews.
  • Visualised price distribution, price vs. review-count relationships, and pricing variation across NYC neighbourhoods.
  • Applied NumPy for array creation, reshaping, slicing and vectorised statistical computation as a separate exercise in the same project.

Project 4

COVID-19 Global Data & Vaccination Progress Analysis

Python · Pandas · Seaborn · Matplotlib

Independent Data Analysis Project — Jupyter Notebook

Combined two large public datasets — global COVID-19 case/death data and global vaccination data (sourced from Our World in Data, in collaboration with the University of Oxford) — into a single merged dataset, then explored relationships between case rates, mortality, vaccination progress and socioeconomic indicators such as GDP and population density.

Data Merging Time-Series Analysis Correlation Analysis 12+ Chart Types
  • Merged two datasets (166,326 rows × 67 columns, and a 15-column vaccination dataset) into a single 81-column analytical dataset, parsing and standardising dates across both sources.
  • Explored correlations between new cases, new deaths, total cases and total deaths via a correlation heatmap, and examined mortality against GDP category, population density and government stringency index.
  • Tracked trends over time — monthly case trends, yearly vaccination totals, and country-level active case trends (e.g. Australia).
  • Produced 15+ distinct visualisations — bar, scatter, pie, box, area, pair plot, heatmap, histogram, line, violin, strip and swarm plots — to communicate findings for different audiences and questions.
